title: 2D Arrays and Matrices
summary: How a matrix is actually laid out in memory, why traversal order changes cache performance, and the in-place transforms interviewers ask for: transpose, 90° rotation, and spiral order.

slides.markdown:
A matrix looks two-dimensional on paper, but memory is one-dimensional — every "2D array" is ultimately a 1D array underneath, addressed with a formula that maps a `(row, col)` pair to a single flat offset.

That one fact explains three things this topic covers: why traversal order changes performance even though it visits the same elements, why in-place transpose and rotation are just index-swapping tricks over that flat layout, and why spiral traversal is really about tracking four shrinking boundaries rather than four separate loops.

slides.subTitle: How (row, col) maps to one address
slides.markdown:
Most languages (C, C++, Java, Python's NumPy by default) store a matrix **row-major**: row 0's elements come first in memory, then row 1's, and so on. The address formula for a `rows × cols` matrix:

```
address(mat[i][j]) = base + (i * cols + j) * element_size
```

This is the exact same idea as 1D array indexing from earlier in this group, just with the row folded into the offset first. A few languages (Fortran, MATLAB, and NumPy when explicitly requested) use **column-major** instead — columns stored contiguously — which flips which traversal order is cache-friendly, covered next.

slides.subTitle: Same result, different cache behavior
slides.markdown:
| Traversal | On a row-major matrix | On a column-major matrix |
|---|---|---|
| Row-by-row (`for i: for j:`) | Sequential memory access — cache-friendly | Strided access — one cache miss per element in the worst case |
| Column-by-column (`for j: for i:`) | Strided access — cache-unfriendly | Sequential memory access — cache-friendly |

Both orders visit every element exactly once and are both O(rows·cols) in Big-O terms — but on a large row-major matrix, row-by-row traversal can be several times faster in wall-clock time than column-by-column, purely from cache locality. This is the array-technique version of the point made in the complexity group: identical Big-O, very different real performance.

slides.sectionTitle: Arrays of arrays vs true contiguous allocation
slides.markdown:
Not every "2D array" is actually one contiguous block. Python's `[[0]*cols for _ in range(rows)]` and Java's `int[rows][cols]` both build an **array of arrays**: one outer array of pointers, each pointing to a separately-allocated row. That extra indirection costs one more memory hop per access — `mat[i][j]` first fetches the pointer to row i, then indexes into that row — and rows aren't guaranteed to sit near each other in memory at all.

A true contiguous 2D allocation (C's `int mat[rows][cols]`, NumPy's default ndarray) has no such indirection — the whole matrix is one flat block, and the row-major formula from the previous slide computes the address directly. This is why NumPy operations on a large matrix can be an order of magnitude faster than the equivalent nested Python lists: not a different algorithm, the same memory-layout gap that separates a dynamic array from a linked list.

slides.subTitle: Swapping across the diagonal
slides.markdown:
Transposing a square matrix (swapping rows and columns, `mat[i][j] ↔ mat[j][i]`) can be done in place because every pair of positions being swapped is disjoint from every other pair — for `i ≠ j`, swapping `(i,j)` with `(j,i)` never collides with swapping `(k,l)` with `(l,k)` for a different pair.

The loop only needs to visit each pair once, not twice — iterate `i` from 0 to n-1 and `j` from `i+1` to n-1, swapping `mat[i][j]` and `mat[j][i]`. Elements on the diagonal (`i == j`) map to themselves and need no swap at all.

slides.subTitle: Transpose, then reverse each row
slides.markdown:
A 90° clockwise rotation of a square matrix decomposes into two operations already covered: **transpose**, then **reverse each row**.

<<< Image: three matrices side by side showing a 3x3 grid with numbers 1-9 in row-major order; first panel is the original; second panel shows the transposed version (rows and columns swapped across the diagonal), labelled "transpose"; third panel shows each row of the transposed matrix reversed left-to-right, labelled "reverse each row", matching the correct 90° clockwise rotation >>>

Why this composition works: transposing puts what should become the first column into the first row (in the wrong left-right order), and reversing each row then fixes that order — the same two-step decomposition idea as the reversal-trick rotation for 1D arrays earlier in this group.

slides.subTitle: 180°, 270°, and counterclockwise
slides.markdown:
Once you have a correct 90° clockwise rotation, the other three rotations are compositions of it rather than new algorithms to derive from scratch:

- **180°** — apply the 90° clockwise rotation twice, or equivalently reverse every row and then reverse the whole matrix top-to-bottom (a direct in-place swap of row i with row n-1-i, then reversing within each row).
- **270° clockwise** (= 90° counterclockwise) — apply the 90° clockwise rotation three times, or derive a direct counterclockwise version by swapping the transpose step's diagonal (transpose across the *anti*-diagonal) and reversing columns instead of rows.
- **Counterclockwise by k·90°** — apply clockwise rotation `(4 - k) % 4` times.

A candidate who's memorized one 90° rotation and can derive the rest from it reads as understanding the structure; one who tries to write four separate rotation functions from scratch under time pressure usually introduces an inconsistency between them.

slides.subTitle: Walking the boundary layer by layer
slides.markdown:
Spiral order visits a matrix's outer ring first (left to right along the top, top to bottom along the right, right to left along the bottom, bottom to top along the left), then repeats for the next ring inward.

Track four shrinking boundaries — `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right` — instead of writing four separate nested loops per layer. Each of the four directional walks moves along one boundary, and after completing a full ring, tighten the corresponding boundaries inward (`top += 1`, `bottom -= 1`, `left += 1`, `right -= 1`) before starting the next ring. The traversal ends when `top > bottom` or `left > right`.

The transpose-then-reverse-rows technique only works for **square** matrices. Rotating a `rows × cols` matrix (rows ≠ cols) by 90° changes its dimensions to `cols × rows` — the output literally doesn't fit in the same backing array, so no in-place algorithm using only that array's existing storage can produce it.

For a non-square matrix, a 90° rotation genuinely requires O(rows·cols) new space for the differently-shaped result — there's no clever index trick around it, because the shape itself changed, not just the contents. Claiming an in-place solution for a non-square rotation is a correctness error, not a missed optimization.

Spiral traversal's most common bug is walking a boundary that's already been fully consumed by a previous direction in the same ring — most often on the final, innermost layer, which can be a single row, a single column, or a single cell.

After walking left-to-right along `top` and top-to-bottom along `right`, the code must check whether `top` still has an un-walked row *before* walking right-to-left along `bottom` (if the ring collapsed to one row, `top == bottom`, and walking bottom again would revisit cells already visited as `top`). The same check is needed before the final upward walk along `left` against `right == left`. Skipping either check either revisits cells (wrong output) or reads past a boundary that's already crossed (index errors) on any matrix with an odd dimension or a single row/column.

slides.subTitle: The nuance behind real matrix-multiply performance
slides.markdown:
Row-major-vs-column-major only tells half the real-world story. Once a matrix is large enough that even one full row doesn't fit in cache, a plain "correct" traversal order stops being enough — production numerical libraries (BLAS implementations behind NumPy, TensorFlow, PyTorch) use **cache blocking (tiling)**: processing the matrix in small sub-blocks that fit entirely in L1/L2 cache before moving to the next block, rather than sweeping full rows or columns straight through.

The payoff is large — a naive triple-nested-loop matrix multiply and a cache-blocked one can differ by 10-50x in wall-clock time on large matrices, despite both being the same O(n³) algorithm. This is the same lesson as elsewhere in this curriculum taken further: Big-O tells you the algorithm is fine; memory hierarchy tells you whether the implementation actually is.
